choices.rationale: Separating decision-makers from cost data removes accountability and delays feedback until the money is already spent.

choices.text: Discuss cost implications during design reviews, in a psychologically safe setting where concerns can be raised
choices.rationale: Individual design decisions affect cost, so cost awareness works best when it is part of how every role designs and reviews.

choices.text: Define a labeling policy and enforce it in Terraform, so costs map to teams and cost centers
choices.rationale: Labels let cost be allocated to departments and cost centers, and automation keeps the labeling consistent.

choices.text: Give each team periodic cost reports and budget or anomaly alerts, built from billing dashboards and BigQuery
choices.rationale: Audience-specific reports and automated notifications give teams the visibility they need to act on their own spend.

choices.text: Restrict billing data to Billing Account Administrators so that the figures people quote stay consistent
choices.rationale: Teams need access to the financial data relevant to their decisions; hiding it prevents ownership.

explanation: FinOps ownership needs allocation (labels), visibility (reports and alerts), and culture (cost in design discussions).

prompt: Cymbal is rolling out a gen AI workflow in which catalog associates approve, reject, or edit generated product attributes. Their current work is manual data entry, and they have heard the program is meant to reduce operating costs, so adoption risk is high. Which two change-management actions best reduce resistance? Choose two.

choices.text: Train associates for the new review and editing tasks, and track adoption KPIs such as review turnaround time and edit rate
choices.rationale: Skills training plus measurable KPIs show progress and identify teams needing help, replacing guesswork about adoption.

choices.text: Keep the cost-reduction rationale confidential and announce the program only after the manual process has been switched off for good
choices.rationale: Withholding the reason until the old process ends erodes trust and gives associates no time to prepare.

choices.text: Make the approval step optional so generated content flows straight to the catalog until associates request review
choices.rationale: Cymbal's requirements call for human review before generated content updates the catalog, so skipping it is not an option.

choices.text: Pilot the review interface with some associates and gather structured feedback from surveys and interviews before the wider rollout
choices.rationale: Early involvement and active feedback let associates shape the tool and surface usability problems before launch.

choices.text: Roll the interface out to every associate on the same day and judge success by comparing headcount before and after
choices.rationale: A big-bang rollout offers no learning loop, and a headcount metric turns a quality program into a threat.

explanation: People-side change needs early involvement, feedback, training, and measurable adoption goals.

prompt: A VP asks for a research-backed way to compare software delivery performance across teams. Which set of metrics does DORA define?

choices.text: Lines of code, commits per developer, story points per sprint, open bug count, and unit test coverage percentage
choices.rationale: These are activity or output measures that are easy to game and are not DORA's delivery performance metrics.

choices.text: Mean time between failures, ticket backlog size, server uptime, patch compliance rate, and the volume of change requests received
choices.rationale: These are traditional operations measures; none captures lead time or deployment frequency, and MTBF is not a DORA metric.

choices.text: CPU utilization, request latency, error rate, saturation, and availability measured per service in production
choices.rationale: These are runtime health signals for a service; they do not measure how effectively a team ships changes.

choices.text: Change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, and deployment rework rate
choices.rationale: These five metrics cover throughput and stability of software delivery and are DORA's published set.

explanation: DORA's metrics measure delivery throughput and stability together, and the research finds speed and stability go together.

prompt: A director reviews last quarter's delivery data for two teams and asks how to improve both. Which interpretation and action is best supported by the data?

exhibit.label: Delivery metrics, last quarter
exhibit.content:
| Team | Deploys per week | Change lead time (commit to production) | Change fail rate | Failed deployment recovery time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atlas | 18 | 2 days | 31% | 6 hours |
| Borealis | 1 | 19 days | 4% | 40 minutes |

choices.text: Atlas ships fast but unstably, so add automated testing and progressive delivery; Borealis is stable but slow, so shrink batch size
choices.rationale: Atlas's 31% change fail rate shows a stability gap, and Borealis's 19-day lead time and weekly-or-less releases show a throughput gap; high performers do well on both.

choices.text: Atlas is the high performer because it deploys most often, so Borealis should copy Atlas's cadence and Atlas needs no change at all
choices.rationale: High deployment frequency with a 31% change fail rate and 6-hour recovery is not high performance; stability counts equally.

choices.text: Borealis is the high performer because its fail rate is lowest, so Atlas should deploy less often to bring its own failures down
choices.rationale: Reducing frequency enlarges batches and risk; DORA research shows speed and stability are not trade-offs, and Borealis's 19-day lead time is poor.

choices.text: Neither team can be assessed until CPU and latency metrics are collected for the services that both teams operate in production
choices.rationale: Delivery performance is measured with lead time, frequency, fail rate, and recovery time, which the table already provides.

explanation: Read DORA metrics as a set: throughput and stability both matter, and the fix for each gap differs.

prompt: Meridian Insurance last exercised its failover 14 months ago. Since then it moved its databases to a new engine and changed its network layout. Which two practices follow Google Cloud guidance on testing recovery? Choose two.

choices.text: Schedule periodic tests, such as quarterly, of failover, rollback, and restore, and repeat them after major infrastructure or software changes
choices.rationale: Guidance calls for periodic testing under changing conditions such as infrastructure changes and software updates, covering failover, rollback, and restore.

choices.text: Check during each test that measured recovery time and data loss meet RTO and RPO, then present a postmortem to stakeholders
choices.rationale: Tests should validate RTO and RPO and data integrity, and share outcomes and lessons learned with stakeholders.

choices.text: Treat a successful backup job as proof that restores work, and exercise restores only after a real incident has occurred
choices.rationale: Completion of a backup job does not prove data can be restored within RTO; restores need to be tested regularly.

choices.text: Run recovery tests without telling operations or application owners, so that the response reflects real conditions on the day itself
choices.rationale: Operations, DevOps, and application owners should be informed of schedule, scope, and potential impact before tests.

choices.text: Test once when the architecture is designed, and retest only if the primary or recovery region is replaced by another one
choices.rationale: Infrastructure and software changes can silently break recovery; a one-time test grows stale as the system evolves.

explanation: Recovery plans decay; test on a cadence, after changes, against measured RTO and RPO, with stakeholders informed.

prompt: A manufacturer replicates on-premises ERP data to Google Cloud and plans a warm recovery environment for the loss of its data center. Which three actions belong in the DR plan? Choose three.

choices.text: Provide an alternative way to reach Google Cloud in case the primary Interconnect or VPN path to the data center fails
choices.rationale: Disaster scenarios may take out the normal access path, so plans need an alternate route to Google Cloud.

choices.text: Rely on the daily VPN or Interconnect connection as the only access path, since the plan assumes the on-premises network survives
choices.rationale: The scenario being planned for is loss of the data center, so a path that depends on it cannot be the only way in.

choices.text: Map on-premises functional roles to IAM policies in the recovery environment, and confirm responders can reach what they need
choices.rationale: Permissions that exist only on-premises will block recovery unless equivalent IAM policies are set up and tested.

choices.text: Grant every responder the Owner role on the recovery project so that permissions can never delay a failover
choices.rationale: Blanket Owner access violates least privilege; the plan should map the roles people actually need.

choices.text: Confirm that the Compute Engine resources needed for recovery will be available in the chosen region, including quota
choices.rationale: A recovery environment is only usable if the needed machine types and quota are actually available when it is activated.

explanation: Hybrid DR plans must cover access, permissions, and capacity in the recovery environment, not only data replication.

prompt: Harbor Payments runs its ledger on Cloud SQL for MySQL with a cross-region read replica for DR and a replication lag of a few seconds. A faulty release ran an UPDATE at 14:02 that corrupted about 2% of rows, and it was noticed at 14:40. The replica holds the same corrupted rows. Which addition best addresses this class of failure?

choices.text: Add a second cross-region replica so that one of the two replicas can be promoted once the corruption has been detected
choices.rationale: Every replica receives the same bad UPDATE, so another copy only multiplies the corrupted data.

choices.text: Tighten replication lag alerts to one second so that corruption is caught before it can reach the replica at all
choices.rationale: Lag alerts measure delivery delay, not data correctness, and cannot identify a logically bad but valid statement.

choices.text: Automated backups with point-in-time recovery, so the ledger can be restored to just before 14:02 as well as the replica
choices.rationale: Replication copies logical corruption as faithfully as good data; point-in-time recovery from backups and binary logs rewinds to a state before the bad change.

choices.text: Switch the replica to synchronous replication so that the DR copy always matches the primary exactly at every moment
choices.rationale: Matching the primary exactly means copying the corruption even faster, which does not give a clean recovery point.

explanation: Replication addresses infrastructure loss; recovering from logical corruption needs backups and point-in-time recovery.

prompt: EHR Healthcare's leadership cites outages caused by misconfiguration and the burden of managing similar-but-separate environments. As the company stands up dev, staging, and production environments on Google Cloud, which process change best addresses this?

choices.text: Define each environment in Terraform under version control, apply it through CI/CD, and reuse modules with per-environment variables
choices.rationale: Infrastructure as code with version control and automated pipelines gives consistent, repeatable, reviewable environments and an easy rollback path.

choices.text: Clone the production project's settings through the console and tweak each copy until its application works as expected
choices.rationale: Console cloning and ad hoc tweaks leave no reviewable record, so environments drift and differences are untraceable.

choices.text: Document the build as a detailed runbook and have the on-call engineer follow it by hand each time an environment is created for a team
choices.rationale: Manual runbooks reintroduce human error and drift between environments, which is the source of the misconfiguration outages.

choices.text: Give each regional team its own tooling and templates so that environments can evolve independently to suit local needs
choices.rationale: Separate templates multiply the number of similar-but-different environments instead of consolidating them.

explanation: Version-controlled infrastructure as code applied by pipelines is how consistency and safe change are enforced.
